https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Barnaby Joyce and Pauline Hanson have stayed at One Nation backer Gina Rinehart’s $20m home in Brisbane, without declaring the hospitality to parliament. Composite: Victoria Hart/Guardian design/AAP View image in fullscreen Barnaby Joyce and Pauline Hanson have stayed at One Nation backer Gina Rinehart’s $20m home in Brisbane, without declaring the hospitality to parliament. Composite: Victoria Hart/Guardian design/AAP One Nation Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce stayed at Gina Rinehart’s $20m mansion after One Nation fundraisers Exclusive: New details underscoring depth of relationship between billionaire and party revealed in first episode of Guardian podcast The Populist Listen to the Guardian’s podcast The Populist here Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Sarah Martin Senior correspondent Sun 13 Sep 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 11.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce stayed overnight at Gina Rinehart’s $20m Brisbane mansion after fundraising events held for One Nation, Guardian Australia can reveal. On one occasion, Joyce conducted a live television interview with Channel Seven’s Sunrise program from a room that appears to be a bedroom in Rinehart’s home. The interview took place on Monday 13 April, the morning after a fundraising event at the mining magnate’s house on the banks of the Brisbane River in Hawthorne. The new details underscoring the depth of the relationship between Australia’s richest person and One Nation have been revealed in the first episode of the Guardian’s new podcast about the party, The Populist , released on Monday. Parliamentary expenditure records show that Hanson and Joyce declared flights on 13 April courtesy of Hancock Prospecting, with flight-tracking data showing that the pair flew on Rinehart’s luxury Gulfstream jet from Brisbane to Sydney that afternoon. View image in fullscreen Barnaby Joyce speaks to Channel Seven’s Sunrise program from Gina Rinehart’s house The accommodation at Rinehart’s home has not been declared to the parliament, which has rules in place mandating that gifts or hospitality valued at more than $300 – or any interest “where a conflict of interest with a [parliamentarian]’s public duties could foreseeably arise or be seen to arise” – should be declared. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here The guidelines state that “hospitality” refers to “free or concessional accommodation” provided to the MP, the MP’s spouse or partner or dependent children “wholly or partly by any person, organisation, business or interest group or foreign government or its representative”. The provision of meals or accommodation excludes “hospitality provided in a purely social way by friends or colleagues”, but the guidelines are designed to place on the public record interests that may conflict, or be seen to conflict, with an MP’s public duty. Joyce told Guardian Australia that Rinehart “was a long-term friend over decades not a motel”. “When I stay with family or friends they don’t charge me, nor do I see it as work,” he said. “I will never be ashamed of doing the research to do a better job.” Guardian Australia can also reveal that Hanson has been using one of Rinehart’s bodyguards for her personal security. The man, who has been seen escorting Hanson in Perth and Canberra, has been one of Rinehart’s closest bodyguards for more than a decade. The New South Wales supreme court heard in 2013 that Rinehart had asked the bodyguard to offer one of her daughters, Bianca Rinehart, a $25m loan to pull out of a court battle contesting the family trust. The offer was rejected. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Politics, really Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you after newsletter promotion Pauline Hanson’s One Nation banks millions in public funding. Where does all the money go? Read more According to his LinkedIn, the man works as a security manager with an undeclared company but a post from 2023 shows him listed as an employee of Hancock Energy. It is unclear if he remains employed by Hancock Prospecting. Guardian Australia has previously reported multiple breaches of Senate rules, with One Nation failing to declare flights gifted by Hancock Prospecting to Hanson going back to August last year. The fresh details of the company’s financial support for One Nation come despite Hanson telling reporters in February she was not being funded by Rinehart, and after the party’s national director, James Ashby, said in December last year: “We have not seen any money from her.” The Labor senator Murray Watt criticised Hanson for failing to disclose the links between her party and Rinehart, including the undeclared flights. “I think that the lengths that she and her colleagues have gone repeatedly to conceal donations, staffing matters, all sorts of other things about their operations, it does make you think that there’s something to hide,” Watt told the Guardian. “In a democratic system like Australia, there is a responsibility of politicians to be transparent about decision making, about their operations, and again Pauline Hanson seems to want to get all the benefits of power without any of the responsibilities of power. “The level of concealment that goes on suggests a guilty conscience. “I think that one of the reasons that One Nation goes to such efforts to conceal their financial gain from Gina Rinehart and her companies is because there is such a close alignment between what Gina Rinehart and Hancock want to see happen and One Nation’s policies.” One Nation did not respond to questions from Guardian Australia. A spokesperson for Hancock Prospecting said: “Donations will be disclosed in accordance with applicable laws and reporting requirements.” Explore more on these topics One Nation Pauline Hanson Barnaby Joyce Gina Rinehart Australian political donations Australian politics Business news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Australia World AU politics Environment Climate crisis Indigenous Australia Immigration Media Business Health Science Tech Podcasts Newsletters

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text: The DPC found that Google users could have been unaware of how their data was being used. Photograph: Aleksandra Michalska/Reuters View image in fullscreen The DPC found that Google users could have been unaware of how their data was being used. Photograph: Aleksandra Michalska/Reuters Google Google fined more than €400m by Irish regulator over its use of location data Watchdog says users may have been unaware their information was used to target adverts or infer their interests Lisa O’Carroll Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.57 BST Last modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 12.40 BST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Google has been fined more than €400m (£345m) over the way it processed users’ location data, following claims that the tech giant had manipulated users into agreeing to be constantly tracked on their mobile phones. The fine, imposed by Ireland’s Data Protection Commission (DPC), comes after complaints from multiple European consumer organisations that Google was following every step users took. Location-related adverts are familiar to holidaymakers, but seven European consumer organisations had complained that undue use of location data can also lead to a breach of privacy . The DPC inquiry was prompted by research by the Norwegian consumer agency in 2018 which suggested location data could reveal details such as religious beliefs (by tracking places of worship), political leanings (for example knowing a user has gone to demonstrations), health conditions (if a user has gone to hospital) and sexual orientation (if they have gone to certain bars). The DPC launched its inquiry six years ago and set out to find out whether Google had a valid legal basis for its use of location data. It found that Google users could have been unaware that their location was being used to influence them with adverts or to gather details about their health and interests. “Location data is a type of personal data which is processed by way of location tracking, and includes data collected or processed by Google, which by itself or in conjunction with other information an individual’s location can be inferred,” said Graham Doyle, a deputy commissioner at the DPC. “Location data can bring both benefits and harms to individuals. “It can greatly enhance the utility of online services, but it can also reveal a significant amount of information about an individual, including information that is inherently private,” Doyle added. Responding to the DPC’s ruling, a Google spokeperson said: “This case centres around historical policies that have since been updated. From 2019 onwards, we’ve significantly evolved our practices and launched robust tools that make managing location data simple.” The European Consumer Organisation (BEUC) based its complaint on research by the Forbrukerrådet, the Norwegian consumer agency, which claimed Google used “various tricks” to ensure location history and web and app activity were enabled. “Today marks an important milestone in the effort to protect our rights online. People must be able to understand what they are agreeing to without being deceived or manipulated into making choices they otherwise would never have made,” says Finn Myrstad, director of digital policy at the Norwegian Consumer Council. BEUC said that geolocation data was “one of the most invasive forms of consumer surveillance”. Agustín Reyna, director general of BEUC, welcomed the ruling but said “the time needed to come to this conclusion is disproportionate with the seriousness of the infringement” arguing “late enforcement can be as harmful as no enforcement at all”. The DPC inquiry looked at “web and app activity”, “location history” and “location accuracy” between 25 May 2018 and 4 February 2020. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion Imposing a fine of €403m, the DPC ordered Google to bring its processing into compliance with the EU’s general data protection regulation (GDPR) within six months. It is the fourth-largest fine imposed by the Irish regulator, which has EU-wide responsibility for all the US tech giants with EU headquarters in Ireland. It has previously fined Meta €1.2bn, TikTok €530m and Instagram (also Meta owned) €405m. Doyle said: “The GDPR provides a high level of protection of personal data throughout the EEA, and requires that the processing of personal data must be carried out in a lawful, fair and transparent manner. AI slowdown calls justified but collapse of bubble may be more immediate threat | Heather Stewart Read more “As a result of Google’s failures in this regard, individuals could have been unaware that their location was being used to, for example, influence them with ads or to infer their interests, and could lose control over their personal data. “The retention of users’ location data for longer than necessary aggravated this loss of control,” added Doyle. There are three other ongoing statutory large-scale inquiries open that concern Google, all of which are at an advanced stage. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/05/flyd.text: The co-pilot of the Israel-bound FlyDubai FZ1073 flight planned to crash the aircraft into Tel Aviv’s Ben-Gurion Airport, according to multiple US and Israeli media reports quoting sources close to the multinational investigation.The same reports say the Omani national named by multiple sources as Hamam Al-Hammami was most likely acting alone.After attacking captain Smit Machchhar, Al-Hammami planned to fly the plane toward Ben Gurion Airport using normal approach and landing procedures, then crash it at the last moment, with more than 180 passengers on board. According to Israeli media quoting sources with knowledge of the investigation, the co-pilot had prepared the attack for several months and previously flew to Israel to gather information.Other reports claim that he planned to crash another flight to Tel Aviv earlier this year, but then changed his mind.Israeli Channel 12 also reported that Israel asked the UAE to expand its questioning to include the flight crew, as even more questions emerge about the harrowing minutes between the co-pilot stabbing the captain and the passengers rushing into the cockpit, subduing the attacker and stabilising the plane.In the first comments by Emirati investigators on Saturday, UAE Prosecutor General Hamad Saif al-Shamsi said the co-pilot of FlyDubai flight FZ1073 “attempted to carry out a terrorist attack” when he attacked the flight captain with an axe and tried to take control of the aircraft.The UAE is leading the investigation, and security agencies from four regional countries, including Israel, are working to establish the co-pilot’s motives, aided by the US and other Western governments.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text: Zuckerberg, worth $239bn, according to Forbes, told Meta he was considering moving his primary residence outside California because Prop 40 could expose him to a massive tax liability. Photograph: Godofredo A Vásquez/AP View image in fullscreen Zuckerberg, worth $239bn, according to Forbes, told Meta he was considering moving his primary residence outside California because Prop 40 could expose him to a massive tax liability. Photograph: Godofredo A Vásquez/AP Meta Meta strikes deal with Zuckerberg to protect him from California wealth tax Company says deal will keep its chief executive living in California even if state brings in one-off billionaire tax Business live – latest updates Graeme Wearden Thu 22 Oct 2026 06.10 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Meta has struck a deal with Mark Zuckerberg to protect him from the threat of a California wealth tax targeting billionaires. The social media company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp revealed on Wednesday night that the arrangement would keep its chief executive living in California , where its headquarters are located. Under the deal, Zuckerberg will receive new shares that could be sold to potentially foot a multibillion-dollar tax bill in the event that California passes a one-off billionaire tax. In return, he is committed to remain a resident of the state, or wherever Meta maintains its base, for eight years Californians will vote early next month on Proposition 40 – a one-time 5% tax on the roughly 250 billionaires who live in the state. Zuckerberg, worth $239bn according to Forbes, told Meta he was considering moving his primary residence elsewhere because Prop 40 could expose him to a massive tax liability, potentially forcing him to sell voting shares to pay it. In response, Meta is creating a new class of non-voting shares via a two-for-one stock split for all existing shareholders. This will allow Zuckerberg to sell some of this new class C shares to pay a potential tax bill, without diluting his control of the company. Recent polling has shown that Prop 40 remains short of majority support with voters. Tech billionaires have been spending heavily to fight the measure , including the Google co-founder Sergey Brin, the Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel, and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. Rohit Khanna, the US congressman representing California’s 17th congressional district, has dubbed Prop 40 as a choice between standing with the working class or the oligarchs. “Every society is taxed. The only question is who will pay. In Trump’s America, working people pay more than they should, while billionaires are so unburdened that they are becoming trillionaires. In the America we seek, billionaires and trillionaires will pay their fair share, while working people will be unburdened,” Khanna wrote in the Guardian last week . Meta also reported a 26% rise in revenues for the last quarter to $64.6bn, beating expectations of $63.3bn. But profits fell by 37% to $13bn, dragged down by a $9.9bn charge related to Meta’s landmark lawsuit over child protection and social media addiction failings . In a separate case, a judge in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $25bn on ⁠Wednesday after a trial found the company had misled the public about how it handled Facebook user data. Meta also revealed it had cut its headcount to 66,775 at the end of September, 15% fewer than a year ago. Reuters contributed to this report. https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/11/08/fran.text: Az európai országok, köztük Franciaország is részt vesz majd az oroszok és ukránok között kedden Abu-Dzabiban, amerikai közvetítéssel kezdődő tárgyalásokon – jelentette be Jean-Noël Barrot francia külügyminiszter az Euronews szerint. Eddig arról volt szó, hogy a november 10 és 11 között zajló tárgyalásokon az orosz és ukrán képviselők mellett csak az amerikai közvetítők lesznek még jelen. Azt lehetett még tudni , hogy az amerikai tárgyalók a héten Brüsszelbe utaznak, hogy ott találkozzanak Franciaország, Németország, az Egyesült Királyság, az Európai Unió és a NATO képviselőivel, és megvitassák az Ukrajnának nyújtandó biztonsági garanciákat. Pedig Volodimir Zelenszkij ukrán elnök egyértelműen amellett volt, hogy Kijev európai szövetségesei is részt vegyenek. Úgy tűnik, hogy ez mégis így is lesz. „Az elmúlt hetekben az európaiak hallatták a hangjukat. Elmagyarázták az amerikai közvetítőknek, hogy a kontinens jövőjéről szóló vita során nem hagyhatjuk figyelmen kívül az elvárásainkat és a követeléseinket” – mondta a francia külügyminiszter. Az Euronews szerint miután csütörtökön találkozott Kirill Dmitrijev orosz nagykövettel, Donald Trump a sajtónak „jelentős megállapodást” helyezett kilátásba, aminek szerinte mindenki örülni fog. Részleteket nem osztott meg. Arról, hogy a félidős vereség után hogyan állhat hozzá a háborús felekhez Trump, ebben a cikkben írtunk bővebben. Jean-Noël Barrot vasárnap azt mondta, hogy nem tudja, mit gondol az amerikai elnök, de szerinte nem lehet kihagyni az európaiakat egy olyan vitából, ami az európai biztonsági architektúrára is kihat. Hozzátette, hogy nem tudja, hogy a franciákat ki fogja képviselni – tehát könnyen lehet, hogy EU-s diplomáciai küldött –, de valaki biztosan ott lesz.
